0: A high-performance ternary blend (353/47/267 cement/fly ash/slag) with an ultra-low W/B of 0.21, enabled by 7.33 kg/m³ HRWR. This mix achieves rapid early strength (5,000 psi at day 1) and 10,290 psi at 28 days — among the top performers in the Set 1 mortar series. The heavy slag component (40% of binder) drives excellent long-term strength development through latent hydraulic reaction, while the low water content creates a dense, low-porosity matrix.
1: A balanced ternary blend with nearly equal parts fly ash (220) and slag (232), and only 215 kg/m³ cement — achieving 67% SCM replacement. Despite this aggressive cement reduction, it reaches 6,222 psi at 28 days. The W/B of 0.24 with 4.4 kg/m³ HRWR provides workability without sacrificing density. A strong sustainability candidate with moderate strength.
2: An exploratory high-water mix (W/B = 0.45) with no superplasticizer, testing the limits of workability-driven design. With 344 kg/m³ cement and 179 fly ash / 144 slag, the high water content creates significant capillary porosity. The result: modest 1,506 psi at day 1, but steady development to 6,276 psi at 28 days as pozzolanic reactions gradually fill pores with C-S-H gel.
3: Similar binder composition to Mix 1 (212/215/240) but with higher water (W/B = 0.26) and no HRWR. Achieves only 4,433 psi at 28 days — notably plateauing between day 3 and 28, suggesting the reaction products may have exhausted available space or reactants. An interesting comparison point showing how even small W/B differences impact long-term development.
4: A fly-ash-rich blend (317/221/128) at W/B = 0.35. Without superplasticizer, this mix relies on the ball-bearing effect of fly ash spheres for workability. Reaches 7,243 psi at 28 days — a strong result given the high water content, demonstrating effective synergy between the three binder components.
5: High-cement design (455 kg/m³, 68% of binder) with significant fly ash (159) but minimal slag (53). The W/B of 0.23 with HRWR produces excellent early strength (6,279 psi at day 1) — the highest 1-day value in the early experimental series. The cement-heavy approach maximizes C₃S hydration for rapid hardening, though at higher GWP cost.
6: A cement-heavy mix (436 kg/m³) with moderate slag (197) but very little fly ash (33). The high W/B of 0.38 without HRWR explains the moderate performance — 3,411 psi at day 1 growing to 6,647 at 28 days. The slag provides late-age strength contribution that partially compensates for the elevated porosity.
7: The highest W/B in the early series (0.48) with moderate binder (319/52/296). At this water content, capillary porosity severely limits strength — only 1,659 psi at day 1. However, the slag-rich binder (44% slag) delivers excellent long-term gain, reaching 5,786 psi at 28 days (3.5× the 1-day value), demonstrating slag's superior densification over time.
8: A well-balanced ternary design (265/164/237, W/B = 0.28) with modest HRWR. Achieves 3,532 psi at day 1 and an impressive 8,685 psi at 28 days — a 2.5× development ratio that highlights the powerful late-age pozzolanic contribution from the combined fly ash + slag system. One of the better strength-to-sustainability ratios in the mortar series.
9: Pure cement + slag binary blend (530/0/137, W/B = 0.41). The very high cement content with zero fly ash produces decent early strength (3,273 psi) but the elevated water limits 28-day performance to 6,674 psi. This mix demonstrates that simply adding more cement without controlling W/B is not an efficient path to high strength.
10: A high-cement + fly ash binary (503/164/0, W/B = 0.36). Without slag, this mix relies entirely on cement hydration and fly ash pozzolanic reaction. Achieves 4,106 psi at day 1 and 7,348 at 28 days. The absence of slag means less late-age hydraulic contribution, making it somewhat cement-efficiency-limited.
11: Binary cement + slag (495/0/171, W/B = 0.45). Very similar to Mix 9 but with more slag and higher water. Performance is slightly lower (6,424 psi at 28 days), confirming that W/B dominates over modest compositional changes when water content is elevated.
12: High-cement binary with fly ash (554/113/0, W/B = 0.35). The highest cement content in the ternary exploration series. Despite this, 28-day strength (7,659 psi) is not exceptional — the relatively low SCM content means less pozzolanic densification over time. A high-GWP baseline comparator.
13: Binary cement + slag with equal parts (334/0/333, W/B = 0.40). A 50-50 cement-slag split at moderate water. Reaches 7,434 psi at 28 days despite no superplasticizer — a testament to slag's hydraulic activity when present in sufficient quantity. The steady strength gain from 2,298 (day 1) suggests ongoing slag hydration well past 28 days.
14: The first of the 'optimized' HRWR series — 467 kg/m³ cement with 200 slag at ultra-low W/B (0.20) and maximum HRWR (9.53 kg/m³). Result: 7,571 psi at day 1 and 10,801 at 28 days. This establishes the performance ceiling for cement-heavy mixes with aggressive water reduction. High GWP but remarkable strength.
15: Similar to Mix 14 but with partial cement replaced by slag (412/29/226, W/B = 0.20). The slight fly ash addition (29 kg/m³) is minimal. Achieves 6,048 psi at day 1 and 10,182 at 28 days — nearly matching Mix 14 with 12% less cement, demonstrating that slag effectively replaces clinker at these low W/B ratios.
16: Continued cement reduction (363/43/261) at the same ultra-low W/B = 0.20 with max HRWR. An unusual strength curve — reaches 10,335 psi at day 5 (!) then slightly retreats to 10,148 at 28 days. This anomalous plateau may indicate early microcracking from rapid hydration heat or measurement variability. Still an exceptional performer.
17: Aggressive SCM replacement (277/118/271, 58% SCMs) at W/B = 0.20. The lowest cement content in the optimized HRWR series. Despite this, achieves 11,198 psi at 28 days — the highest in this sub-group! This demonstrates the remarkable finding that heavy SCM replacement at very low W/B can actually exceed high-cement mixes. A key result supporting the project's sustainability thesis.
18: A moderate-SCM ternary (201/173/293, W/B = 0.25) with reduced HRWR (3.67 kg/m³). Only 30% cement by binder weight. Reaches 8,588 psi at 28 days with good late development (3,105 → 8,588). This formulation becomes a recurring basis for later optimization rounds, suggesting the BO algorithm identified this region as promising.
19: Refined version of the ternary concept (322/83/262, W/B = 0.22) with high HRWR (7.33). Achieves an impressive 11,900 psi at 28 days — among the best in the mortar series. The strength development from 5,776 (day 1) to 11,900 (day 28) shows both rapid early hydration and strong late pozzolanic contribution. Excellent balance of sustainability and performance.
20: Slag-dominant variant (293/73/300, W/B = 0.20, max HRWR). With 45% slag and only 44% cement by binder, this pushes toward high sustainability. Reaches 10,043 psi at 28 days — still excellent. The high slag content with ultra-low W/B creates a dense, durable matrix with low permeability.
21: Maximum slag (300 kg/m³) with moderate fly ash (137) and low cement (229, only 34% of binder). At W/B = 0.20 with max HRWR, achieves 9,226 psi at 28 days. Demonstrates that even at 66% SCM replacement, ultra-low W/B maintains excellent performance. Late-age strength gain (3,768 → 9,226) is dramatic.
22: Cement-leaning variant (395/45/226, 59% OPC) at W/B = 0.20 with max HRWR. The higher cement fraction produces rapid early strength (5,654 psi day 1) but 28-day result (9,696 psi) is slightly below the more sustainable Mix 17 (11,198 psi). Further evidence that more cement ≠ more strength at these conditions.
23: Balanced design (305/126/236, 46% cement) at ultra-low W/B with max HRWR. Reaches 10,305 psi at 28 days with excellent uniformity in strength gain. At only 46% cement content, this achieves performance rivaling much higher-cement formulations — a strong sustainability case study.
24: Higher-cement formulation (408/109/150) with max HRWR but only 22% slag. The reduced slag means less late-age contribution, reflected in the 9,224 psi at 28 days — good but below the slag-rich mixes. An interesting data point showing slag's value at these ultra-low W/B conditions.
25: Well-balanced mid-range (341/101/225, 51% cement) with max HRWR. Achieves an outstanding 10,569 psi at 28 days. The balanced binder with ultra-low W/B hits a sweet spot — enough cement for early strength (4,939 psi day 1) plus sufficient slag for late-age densification. A top performer.
26: Lower total binder (273/81/180 = 534 kg/m³) with max HRWR. Even with less total cite material, the ultra-low W/B (0.25) delivers 7,950 psi at 28 days. This tests whether reducing overall binder can maintain performance — it does, moderately, suggesting some inefficiency in very high binder mixes.
27: Same binder as Mix 21 (229/137/300) but at higher W/B (0.30) without HRWR. A direct comparison: removing HRWR and raising water drops 28-day strength from 9,226 to 8,599 psi — a smaller penalty than expected. This suggests the binder composition itself is robust, maintaining good performance across a range of W/B ratios.
28: Same binder as Mix 27 but with fly ash and slag swapped (229/300/137). At W/B = 0.30 without HRWR, achieves only 6,145 psi at 28 days — significantly less than the slag-dominant Mix 27 (8,599 psi). This reveals that slag is the more effective SCM at these proportions, likely due to its latent hydraulic activity vs fly ash's slower pozzolanic mechanism.
29: Lower binder content (161/138/235 = 534 kg/m³) with reduced HRWR (3.67) and higher fine aggregate (1967 kg/m³). At W/B = 0.31, reaches 6,521 psi at 28 days. This tests aggregate-rich formulations that reduce paste volume. Good late strength development (1,454 → 6,521, a 4.5× ratio) suggests the binder is working efficiently.
30: High-binder version (241/207/352 = 800 kg/m³) with lower aggregate (1700) and modest HRWR. Despite W/B = 0.21, achieves an excellent 11,357 psi at 28 days. The very high total binder content with heavy SCM loading (70% replacement) creates a dense matrix. The extraordinary development from 3,424 (day 1) to 11,357 (day 28) showcases the power of combined slag + fly ash pozzolanic reactions.
31: An extreme ultra-low W/B experiment: 400 kg/m³ pure cement at W/B = 0.20 with max HRWR (11.73) and very high aggregate (2100 kg/m³). Essentially an ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC) formulation. Only reaches 3,779 psi at 28 days — surprisingly low. The extremely low water may have left insufficient moisture for complete hydration, or the high aggregate fraction created poor paste distribution.
32: Ultra-low binder, ultra-low water design: only 229 kg/m³ pure cement at W/B = 0.20 with max HRWR and extremely high aggregate (2271 kg/m³). A very lean paste attempting UHPC-like performance. Only achieves 1,422 psi at 28 days — the cement-deficient paste cannot develop adequate strength. This maps the failure boundary of minimal binder design.
33: Extremely low total binder (123/32/55 = 210 kg/m³) at W/B = 0.20 with max HRWR. Very aggregate-rich (2289 kg/m³). Only 1,209 psi at 28 days — as expected for such low binder content. This is a boundary-exploration mix establishing the minimum binder needed for structural integrity.
34: Near-zero cement design (97/3/71 = 171 kg/m³ total binder) with W/B = 0.49. The highest aggregate loading (2329 kg/m³) and almost no binder. Only 1,022 psi at 28 days. An extreme data point testing how little binder can function — essentially a lean mortar approaching aggregate-only behavior.
35: Moderate-binder formulation (315/112/49) at high aggregate (2025) with max HRWR and low W/B = 0.24. The fly-ash-rich SCM system reaches 6,866 psi at 28 days — respectable for a practical concrete (vs mortar) formulation. This begins the transition toward real-world deployable designs.
36: Cement-dominant (367/25/25, 88% OPC) at very low W/B = 0.20 with max HRWR and high aggregate. Despite the near-pure cement approach, only reaches 6,088 psi at 28 days. Comparison with Mix 35 (more SCMs, better performance) reinforces that SCMs add value even in aggregate-rich concretes.
37: Ultra-low binder (67/68/9 = 144 kg/m³) at W/B = 0.31 with max HRWR. Only 529 psi at 28 days — practically zero strength at day 1. This extreme low-binder design demonstrates the absolute minimum paste volume where cementitious activity is essentially negligible. A boundary condition for the GP model.
38: Pure high-cement design (499/0/0) at W/B = 0.20 with max HRWR. A reference mix establishing the Portland-cement-only performance ceiling at high aggregate content. Achieves 8,455 psi at 28 days — strong, but notably surpassed by several SCM-blended mixes that use half the cement. An important baseline showing that SCMs don't just save CO₂ — they can improve performance.
39: Very low binder (160/13/16 = 189 kg/m³) at extremely high aggregate content (2311 kg/m³). Only 845 psi at 28 days. Another low-binder boundary point — minimal paste simply cannot develop meaningful strength regardless of W/B optimization.
40: A practical blend (335/104/51) at low W/B with max HRWR. Achieves 8,446 psi at 28 days — matching the pure cement Mix 38 but with 33% less cement. The fly ash provides workability benefits and pozzolanic strengthening at this reduced W/B. A strong sustainability argument in one comparison.
41: Extremely high cement content (887 kg/m³!) with minimal SCMs (9 fly ash, 56 slag). W/B = 0.26 with moderate HRWR (2.93). This is an outlier exploring ultra-high binder loading. Achieves 8,235 psi at 28 days — but with an unusual flat curve (7,863 at day 1, only 5% gain to day 28). The enormous cement content provides rapid early reaction but limited continued development. Also the highest GWP in the dataset (~695 kg CO₂/m³).
42: Sister mix to 41 (895/25/59) at slightly lower W/B = 0.24. Achieves 10,448 psi at 28 days — better than 41 despite similar composition, likely due to the marginally lower water. Together, 41 and 42 establish the 'brute force cement' performance ceiling and demonstrate diminishing returns beyond ~500 kg/m³ OPC.
43: High-binder ternary (241/207/352 = 800 kg/m³) but at elevated W/B (0.36) without HRWR. The same binder as the excellent Mix 30, but with more water. Reaches 7,027 psi at 28 days vs Mix 30's 11,357 — dramatically demonstrating how W/B ratio dominates. The 5.3× development ratio (1,319 → 7,027) shows the slag system is still working hard at late ages.
44: Mix 21's binder (229/137/300) at W/B = 0.35 without HRWR. Achieves 7,662 psi at 28 days — actually exceeding the higher-water variant Mix 27 (8,599 at W/B 0.30). Excellent late development from 1,518 (day 1), confirming this slag-rich binder's robust performance across water content variations.
45: Moderate binder (316/112/49) at higher water (W/B = 0.35) without HRWR. A 'realistic workability' version of Mix 35. Reaches 6,011 psi at 28 days — reasonable but clearly below the HRWR-optimized version (6,866). The aggregate content is 2025 kg/m³, making this a practical concrete design.
46: An inverted version of Mix 45: slag-dominant (49/112/316) instead of cement-dominant. At W/B = 0.35 without HRWR, achieves only 3,668 psi at 28 days — but at extremely low GWP (73 kg CO₂/m³). This mix sacrifices strength for dramatic sustainability gains, achieving the lowest environmental impact while still reaching structural concrete grade. On the Pareto front because no other mix matches its GWP at any comparable strength.
47: High-SCM, high-aggregate design (253/160/307, 65% SCM) at W/B = 0.35. Reaches 6,594 psi at 28 days with good development. The balanced fly ash + slag system with moderately elevated aggregate creates a practical, lower-carbon formulation. Steady strength gain indicates ongoing pozzolanic activity.
48: Similar to Mix 44 but with higher aggregate (229/164/273, W/B = 0.35). Achieves 6,798 psi at 28 days. The slightly modified aggregate grading and binder proportions produce comparable results, suggesting robustness in this design region.
49: Slag-rich binary (229/0/300) with very low HRWR (1.47) at W/B = 0.38 and increased fine aggregate (1967). No fly ash — relying entirely on slag for supplementary cementing. Reaches 6,903 psi at 28 days. The absence of fly ash means less workability improvement but more direct hydraulic activity from the slag.
50: Binary cement + slag (240/0/433) at W/B = 0.36 without HRWR. Very high slag fraction (64% of binder). Reaches 6,888 psi at 28 days with excellent development (1,324 → 6,888, 5.2×). Demonstrates that slag-only systems can match ternary blends when properly proportioned.
51: Extreme slag exploration (110/0/1156 — 91% slag!) at W/B = 0.35 with reduced fine aggregate (1233). Only 110 kg/m³ cement — the lowest in any mix with significant binder. Reaches only 4,445 psi at 28 days, with very slow early development (286 psi day 1). This maps the extreme end of slag replacement — functional but limited by insufficient alkali activation from the minimal cement.
52: Another high-slag design (169/15/397) at W/B = 0.35. Reaches 6,556 psi at 28 days — substantially better than the extreme Mix 51, showing the importance of minimum cement for activating slag hydration. The 68% slag replacement is more practical while still achieving excellent sustainability.
53: Zero-cement formulation (0/0/1199 — pure slag!) at W/B = 0.24. An extreme experiment: can slag alone, without any Portland cement activator, develop strength? Reaches 3,574 psi at 28 days from essentially zero at day 1. Remarkable that any strength develops without alkali activation — suggests the slag has some self-cementing capability at this finely-ground state.
54: Low-cement slag-rich design (129/3/438, 77% slag) at W/B = 0.40. Achieves 5,952 psi at 28 days with excellent development ratio (611 → 5,952, 9.7×). The minimal cement provides just enough activation for the massive slag content to react over time. One of the highest strength-gain ratios in the dataset.
55: Ternary with very low cement (49/44/632 — 87% slag) at W/B = 0.35. Only 49 kg/m³ cement — among the lowest non-zero values. Reaches 5,012 psi at 28 days. Despite extreme cement reduction, the slag-dominant system develops meaningful strength, with a 24× development from day 1 (210 psi). An extreme sustainability formulation.
56: High-slag with modest cement (195/13/781, 79% slag) at W/B = 0.35 and reduced aggregate (1512). The very high total binder (989 kg/m³) compensates for the extreme slag fraction. Achieves 7,371 psi at 28 days — demonstrating that massive slag with sufficient total paste volume can produce high-strength concrete. Excellent GWP profile.
57: Pure cement reference (667/0/0) at W/B = 0.40 with moderate HRWR (4.0). A high-cement baseline for the mortar series. Achieves 7,822 psi at 28 days — strong early (3,792 day 1) but limited late gain. This pure OPC reference is outperformed by several SCM-blended mixes at lower GWP, reinforcing the project's core finding.
58: Same pure cement (667/0/0) at lower W/B = 0.30 with more HRWR (5.33). Achieves 8,096 psi at 28 days and notably higher early strength (5,070 day 1) vs Mix 57. The W/B reduction from 0.40 to 0.30 provides 4% more 28-day strength and 34% more 1-day strength — confirming W/B as the primary performance lever.
59: Pure cement (667/0/0) at high W/B = 0.50 without HRWR. Two sets of observations exist (replicate testing): first batch reached 5,883 psi, second batch 7,076 psi at 28 days. The variability (~20%) at this high W/B highlights how elevated water content amplifies process sensitivity. A valuable data point for uncertainty quantification.
60: Pure cement (667/0/0) at W/B = 0.40 with reduced HRWR (2.67). Nearly identical to Mix 57 but with slightly less superplasticizer. Achieves 7,076 psi at 28 days — confirming reproducibility in this design space.
61: Pure cement (667/0/0) at W/B = 0.40 with coarse + fine aggregate (611/1176 blend). First mix in the series with both aggregate fractions — transitioning from mortar to concrete. Achieves 7,408 psi at 28 days. The split aggregate creates better particle packing than fine-only designs.
62: Same pure cement (667/0/0) with balanced aggregates at W/B = 0.40 and HRWR 2.138. Now includes 14-day measurement. Achieves 9,491 psi at 28 days — notably higher than Mixes 57-61 despite similar composition. The aggregate optimization appears to improve performance significantly. Steady progression from 4,897 (day 1) to 9,491.
63: Identical formulation to Mix 62 — likely a replicate. Achieves 9,351 psi at 28 days (vs 62's 9,491). Excellent reproducibility, confirming this pure-cement baseline is consistent. The <2% variance provides confidence in the experimental methodology.
64: Another near-replicate of Mix 62-63. Achieves 9,490 psi at 28 days. Three consecutive mixes with essentially identical results (9,351 / 9,490 / 9,491) demonstrate that this formulation is highly reproducible — an important property for deployment confidence.
65: The breakthrough mix: 201/173/293 (30% cement, 70% SCMs) at W/B = 0.25 with balanced aggregates. Achieves a stunning 14,924 psi at 28 days — the second-highest in the entire dataset. More remarkably, early strength is only 901 psi (day 1) — a 16.6× development ratio showing massive late-age pozzolanic reaction. This demonstrates that ultra-high performance is achievable with dramatic cement reduction. A poster child for the sustainable concrete thesis.
66: The dataset champion: same base as Mix 65 but with slightly more HRWR (4.63 vs 3.56 kg/m³). Achieves 16,029 psi at 28 days — the absolute maximum strength observed across all 154 mixes. From only 1,809 psi at day 1, the 8.9× development demonstrates extraordinary late pozzolanic densification. At only 30% cement content, this definitively proves that sustainability and ultra-high performance are not mutually exclusive.
67: High-cement variant (455/159/53) with balanced aggregates at W/B = 0.30. Achieves 11,848 psi at 28 days — strong but notably below the SCM-rich Mixes 65-66 despite 2× the cement content. This comparison is perhaps the single most powerful data point in the dataset: more cement produces less strength than the optimized SCM blend.
68: Ultra-high cement (887/9/55) with balanced aggregates at W/B = 0.30. Essentially pure cement in a concrete matrix. Achieves 9,265 psi at 28 days — very flat curve (5,928 day 1 → 9,265 day 28, only 1.56× ratio). Most strength is achieved early from rapid C₃S hydration with minimal late-age gain. The highest GWP in the concrete series (~691 kg CO₂/m³) yet underperforms Mixes 65-66 by 42%.
69: Mix 65's binder (229/137/300) at higher W/B = 0.30 with HRWR. Achieves 11,548 psi at 28 days — excellent but below Mix 65 (14,924). The W/B increase from 0.25 to 0.30 costs ~23% strength. Dramatic development from 1,022 (day 1) to 11,548 confirms the same powerful late-age mechanism seen in 65-66.
70: Mix 65's binder (201/173/293) cured at -20°C — testing cold-weather performance. Only 2,746 psi at 28 days, with an anomalous strength curve: 2,002 (day 1) → 3,185 (day 3) → 2,969 (day 5) → 2,642 (day 14) → 2,746 (day 28). The sub-zero temperature freezes pore water, halting hydration and potentially causing frost damage. A critical cautionary data point for winter construction.
72: A lower-binder variant (133/167/367 = 667 kg/m³, 80% SCM) at W/B = 0.30 with HRWR. Achieves 8,025 psi at 28 days. The extremely high SCM fraction with very low cement still delivers good performance in this concrete formulation. Development from 413 (day 1) shows the SCM system needs time but delivers reliably.
75: Fly-ash-dominant (133/533/0 — 80% fly ash, zero slag) at W/B = 0.30 with low HRWR. Only 3,243 psi at 28 days. The pure fly ash system without slag lacks hydraulic reactivity — fly ash requires Ca(OH)₂ from cement hydration to react, and with only 20% cement, activation is limited. Demonstrates why slag is preferred over fly ash for high-replacement designs.
76: Ternary (133/233/300) at W/B = 0.30 with low HRWR. Achieves only 3,410 psi at 28 days despite a similar replacement level to the champion mixes. The extremely slow start (133 psi at day 1, 122 at day 3!) suggests the low cement content barely generates enough heat for initial activation. Recovery to 3,410 by day 28 indicates eventual pozzolanic activity.
77: Same binder as Mix 76 at slightly higher W/B (0.30) with higher HRWR. Achieves 11,648 psi at 28 days — even better than 76! Development from 649 (day 1) to 11,648 shows the additional HRWR improved early hydration kinetics. This Pareto-optimal mix delivers near-champion-level strength at 70% cement replacement.
142: Set 3 (161/88/102) at W/B = 0.40 without HRWR. Balanced ternary: 1,068 psi at day 1 (no later measurements). A moderate early-strength data point suggesting reasonable 28-day potential based on similar compositions.
80: Minimal cement (735 day 1, 4,557 day 28) — another reduced binder test. Performance is limited by total paste content rather than W/B or SCM ratio.
82: Similar low-binder design reaching 8,488 psi at 28 days — the best performer in the reduced-binder sub-series. The specific binder proportions and low W/B combine effectively here.
83: Very low cement (84 day 1 strength) indicating extremely slow activation. Reaches 5,490 psi at 28 days — respectable given the minimal cement. The 65× development ratio (84 → 5,490) shows even tiny amounts of cement can eventually activate slag/fly ash reactions.
84: Higher binder design (4,477 psi day 1 → 8,242 day 28) in the Set 3 series with balanced aggregates. A strong baseline performer showing good early and late strength in a practical concrete formulation.
85: Refined design reaching 9,624 psi at 28 days with excellent progressive development (4,295 → 6,831 → 7,726 → 8,509 → 9,624). The steady, monotonic gain indicates healthy ongoing hydration without early-age issues.
86: SCM-rich formulation achieving 10,040 psi at 28 days from only 1,984 at day 1. The 5× development demonstrates powerful pozzolanic activity. Among the best performers in its sub-group, confirming the high-SCM approach works in practical concrete matrices.
87: Strong late-developer: 897 psi (day 1) → 10,380 psi (day 28) — an 11.6× ratio. This extraordinary late-age development is characteristic of the slag-rich formulations that anchor the project's sustainability findings.
88: Moderate performer reaching 7,993 psi at 28 days at very low GWP. The balance of acceptable strength with minimal environmental impact places it on the Pareto front — representing the practical sweet spot where builders don't sacrifice much performance but gain major sustainability benefits.
89: Reaches 6,802 psi at 28 days but with an unusual curve — peaks at ~7,410 (day 14) then drops to 6,802 at day 28. This late-age regression is uncommon and may indicate sulfate-related expansion or delayed ettringite formation affecting long-term stability.
90: Very slow starter (85 psi day 1) but recovers to 5,235 at 28 days. The 62× development ratio indicates this mix needs extended curing to develop useful strength — not ideal for fast-track construction but suitable for mass concrete applications where early strength isn't critical.
91: Set 3 slag-dominant (263/0/108) at W/B = 0.35 with HRWR. Achieves 9,344 psi at 28 days — dramatically better than the fly-ash-only Set 3 mixes (4,000-5,000 range). This confirms that slag is far more effective than fly ash as an SCM in Set 3 materials, likely due to slag's direct hydraulic activity vs fly ash's dependency on Ca(OH)₂ availability.
92: Set 3 high-slag (225/0/223) at W/B = 0.35 with HRWR. Achieves 8,866 psi at 28 days. With 50% slag replacement, maintains excellent performance. The development from 2,178 (day 1) confirms reliable slag activation in Set 3 cement.
93: Set 3 ternary (210/39/122) at W/B = 0.35 with HRWR. Achieves 8,372 psi at 28 days — strong with modest fly ash addition. The slag-cement-fly ash combination works well in Set 3 when slag dominates the SCM fraction.
94: Set 3 (179/0/191) at W/B = 0.35 with HRWR. A near-equal cement-slag binary. Reaches 8,256 psi at 28 days — consistent with the slag-focused Set 3 designs that all cluster around 8,000-9,000 psi.
95: Set 3 (148/0/222) at W/B = 0.35 with HRWR. 60% slag replacement — aggressive but effective. Reaches 7,784 psi at 28 days. Even at this high slag fraction in Set 3, performance remains above typical structural concrete requirements.
96: Set 3 (263/0/108) at higher W/B = 0.40 with low HRWR. Same binder as the excellent Mix 101 but with more water. Drops to 6,757 psi from 9,344 — a 28% penalty. Confirms W/B sensitivity even in the slag-optimized Set 3 formulations.
97: Set 3 (263/0/108) at W/B = 0.45 without HRWR. Further W/B increase reduces 28-day strength to 6,295 psi. The progressive degradation (9,344 → 6,757 → 6,295) quantifies exactly how much performance is sacrificed per unit of W/B increase.
98: Set 3 (263/0/108) at W/B = 0.50 without HRWR. The highest W/B for this binder. Only 4,631 psi — a 50% drop from the optimized version. Demonstrates that even excellent binder compositions fail when water content is excessive.
99: Set 3 (237/0/97) at W/B = 0.39 with HRWR. Slightly lower total binder and slag than Mix 101. Reaches 7,563 psi — moderate-to-good performance consistent with the somewhat leaner paste volume.
100: Set 3 (210/0/86) at W/B = 0.44 with HRWR. Progressive binder reduction series. Achieves 6,926 psi — still acceptable. The HRWR partially compensates for the elevated W/B.
101: Set 3 (184/0/76) at W/B = 0.50 without HRWR. Only 5,235 psi — confirming the combined effect of reduced binder and elevated water.
102: Set 3 (225/0/223) at higher W/B = 0.40 without HRWR. Achieves 6,659 psi — a drop from Mix 102's 8,866 but still solid structural concrete.
103: Set 3 (179/0/191) at W/B = 0.40 with HRWR. Reaches 6,766 psi at 28 days — consistent with the gradual performance decline at elevated W/B in this slag-rich system.
104: Set 3 (179/0/191) at W/B = 0.45 without HRWR. Only 6,229 psi — below the HRWR variants, as expected. Still adequate structural performance.
105: Set 3 (179/0/191) at W/B = 0.50 without HRWR. The bottom of the W/B range for this binder: 4,906 psi. Maps the complete W/B response surface for this specific slag-cement ratio.
106: Set 3 (162/0/172) at W/B = 0.39 with HRWR. Near-equal cement-slag binary at moderate water. Reaches 5,650 psi — decent given the modest binder total (334 kg/m³).
107: Set 3 (144/0/153) at W/B = 0.44 with HRWR. Further reduced total binder. Achieves 6,259 psi — slightly better than Mix 116 despite lower binder, possibly due to better aggregate packing.
108: Set 3 (126/0/134) at W/B = 0.50 with HRWR. Very lean binder (260 kg/m³). Only 5,021 psi. Approaching the minimum viable binder content for structural applications.
109: Set 3 (210/0/86) at W/B = 0.44 with HRWR. Multiple observations (replicate testing) give 6,312 and 5,670 psi — a ~11% variance. This moderate variability is typical and informs the GP model's noise estimation.
110: Set 3 cold-cured (210/0/86 at 10°C) with HRWR. Achieves 5,522 psi at 28 days. Lower than the 22°C versions (~6,000-6,900 range). The slag-cement binary is moderately sensitive to temperature reduction.
111: Set 3 with fly ash (180/30/90) at W/B = 0.44 with HRWR. Adding fly ash to the slag system: 5,370 psi at 28 days. The ternary blend doesn't outperform the binary — suggesting fly ash adds limited value when slag is already present in Set 3 materials.
112: Set 3 higher fly ash (150/60/90) at W/B = 0.44 with HRWR. More fly ash, less cement: only 5,137 psi. Confirms the trend that increasing fly ash at slag's expense doesn't help in Set 3 mixes.
113: Set 3 slag-rich ternary (150/30/120) at W/B = 0.44 with HRWR. Achieves 6,162 psi — better than the fly-ash-heavy variants 121-122. Favoring slag over fly ash continues to win in Set 3.
114: Set 3 higher binder (210/0/90) at low W/B = 0.40 with HRWR. Achieves 8,242 psi — strong, approaching the best Set 3 results. The lower W/B and adequate HRWR produce a dense, high-performance matrix.
115: Set 3 (180/30/90) at low W/B = 0.40 with HRWR. Moderate ternary achieving 6,559 psi. Compared to Mix 124 (8,242 without fly ash), the fly ash substitution costs ~20% strength. Clear evidence that slag > fly ash for Set 3 performance.
116: Set 3 (150/60/90) at low W/B = 0.40 with HRWR. More fly ash substitution: 5,680 psi. Continued confirmation that fly ash dilutes strength in Set 3 at these proportions.
117: Set 3 (150/30/120) at low W/B = 0.40 with HRWR. Slag-favoring ternary: 7,112 psi — 25% better than the fly-ash variant Mix 126. This consistent slag advantage across multiple conditions is a clear finding for Set 3 material optimization.
118: Set 3 (245/0/105) at W/B = 0.44 with HRWR. Higher cement, lower slag: 6,687 psi at 28 days. A moderate-performing Set 3 concrete suitable for typical structural applications.
119: Set 3 (210/30/60) at W/B = 0.44 with HRWR. Lower slag with modest fly ash: 5,968 psi. Mid-range performer in the Set 3 optimization series.
120: Set 3 (180/30/90) at W/B = 0.44 with different HRWR dosage. Achieves 5,490 psi — consistent with other mixes in this composition region.
121: Set 3 (180/30/90) at W/B = 0.40 with HRWR and slightly different aggregate ratio. Reaches 6,425 psi. The lower W/B provides the expected improvement over the 0.44 variants.
122: Set 3 (245/35/70) at W/B = 0.44 with HRWR. Moderate ternary: 5,679 psi at 28 days. The modest SCM content keeps this in the mid-range of Set 3 performance.
123: Set 3 (210/35/105) at W/B = 0.44 with HRWR. Balanced ternary achieving 5,881 psi — consistent with the surrounding design space.
124: Set 3 (210/35/105) at lower W/B = 0.40 with HRWR. Achieves 5,929 psi — slightly better than Mix 133's 5,881, confirming the modest benefit of W/B reduction.
125: Set 3 with high fly ash (165/186/0 — 53% fly ash, zero slag) at W/B = 0.40 without HRWR. Only 3,810 psi at 28 days. This zero-slag, high-fly-ash design further confirms that Set 3 benefits far more from slag than fly ash. A clear negative result guiding away from fly-ash-heavy formulations.
126: Set 3 (210/0/140) at W/B = 0.40 with HRWR. Slag-only SCM: 6,325 psi at 28 days. Compared to Mix 135 (fly-ash-only, 3,810 psi), this conclusively demonstrates the 66% strength advantage of slag over fly ash in Set 3 mixes — one of the clearest comparative findings in the dataset.
127: Set 3 (305/0/46) at W/B = 0.40 with HRWR. High cement with minimal slag: 7,046 psi. Among the best Set 3 results without aggressive W/B reduction. The high cement content (87% of binder) compensates for the minimal SCM contribution.
128: Set 3 low-cement slag-rich (95/0/256) at W/B = 0.40 with HRWR. Only 27% cement by binder. Reaches 4,902 psi — modest but impressive given the extreme cement reduction. The slag carries most of the load.
129: Set 3 very low cement (105/21/224) at W/B = 0.47 without HRWR. Only 30% cement, high water: 4,064 psi. Acceptable structural concrete from minimal cement — demonstrating viability of high-replacement Set 3 designs.
130: Set 3 ternary (126/35/189) at W/B = 0.40 with HRWR. Slag-dominant with modest fly ash: 5,749 psi. Solid mid-range performance at 64% SCM replacement.
131: Set 3 (63/56/231) at W/B = 0.40 with HRWR. Only 18% cement! Achieves 4,293 psi at very low GWP. Pareto-optimal because it achieves reasonable structural strength at near-minimal environmental impact for Set 3 mixes. A practical low-carbon formulation for less demanding applications.
132: Set 3 ternary (95/67/189) at W/B = 0.40 with HRWR. 27% cement: reaches 4,986 psi at 28 days. Good balance of sustainability and adequate structural performance.
133: Set 3 (130/154/67) at W/B = 0.40 without HRWR. Fly-ash-dominant SCM: only 3,349 psi. Another data point confirming the inferior performance of fly-ash-heavy Set 3 formulations compared to slag-rich ones.
134: Set 3 (81/144/126) at W/B = 0.40 without HRWR. Balanced fly ash + slag at very low cement (23%): 3,722 psi. Modest but functional. The combination of both SCMs performs slightly better than fly ash alone (Mix 143).
135: Set 3 (70/235/46) at W/B = 0.40 without HRWR. Extremely fly-ash-heavy (67% of binder) with minimal slag. Only measured to 14 days (2,008 psi). Despite low performance, this may be Pareto-optimal at the extreme low-GWP end of the Set 3 frontier.
136: Set 3 (116/196/39) at W/B = 0.40 without HRWR. High fly ash: 2,908 psi at 14 days (no 28-day data). Performance limited by the fly-ash-dominated system in Set 3.
137: Set 3 (81/186/84) at W/B = 0.40 without HRWR. Mixed SCMs: 2,997 psi at 14 days. Mid-range for the high-SCM Set 3 exploration.
138: Set 3 (147/172/32) at W/B = 0.40 without HRWR. Fly-ash-heavy: 3,243 psi at 14 days. All the fly-ash-dominant Set 3 mixes cluster around 2,000-3,500 psi — consistently below the slag-rich equivalents.
139: Set 3 (175/140/35) at W/B = 0.40 without HRWR. Moderate fly ash with more cement: 3,643 psi at 14 days. Slightly better due to higher cement, but still limited by the fly ash system.
140: Set 3 (158/133/60) at W/B = 0.40 without HRWR. Balanced design: 4,119 psi at 14 days. The best in the zero-HRWR, zero-slag-emphasis Set 3 group — likely benefiting from the higher cement fraction.
141: Set 3 (70/21/259) at W/B = 0.40 with HRWR. Slag-dominant with only 20% cement. Only day 1 measurement: 360 psi. Extremely slow-starting but potentially strong at late ages (unmeasured). Pareto-optimal at the extreme low-GWP boundary for Set 3 where minimal cement and maximum slag create the lowest possible carbon footprint for a cementitious material.
143: Set 3 (137/123/91) at W/B = 0.40 without HRWR. Balanced ternary: 780 psi at day 1 (no later measurements). The lower cement content vs Mix 152 is reflected in the lower 1-day strength.
71: High-SCM ternary blend (201/173/293 cement/fly ash/slag) at W/B = 0.40 without HRWR. At 70% SCM replacement, the slag-dominant system still achieves 8,294 psi at 28 days — demonstrating that well-proportioned slag/fly ash combinations can deliver excellent late-age strength with significantly reduced GWP (189 kg CO₂/m³).
73: Moderate-SCM blend (455/159/53) at low W/B = 0.30, cured at -20°C. Cold curing severely retards hydration kinetics, limiting 28-day strength to 4,981 psi despite favorable binder proportions. The Arrhenius relationship predicts much higher strength at standard temperature — this data point quantifies the cold-curing penalty.
74: Pure cement (667/0/0) at W/B = 0.40 cured at -20°C. Only 3,038 psi at 28 days — a dramatic reduction from the same mix at standard temperature. Without SCMs to contribute to long-term strength, and with severe cold retardation, early hydration products form slowly and the microstructure remains porous. The highest GWP (514 kg CO₂/m³) in the dataset with the worst cold-curing performance.
78: Same binder as index 71 (201/173/293) but at lower W/B = 0.35 with HRWR. The 0.05 reduction in W/B boosts 28-day strength by 19% (9,849 vs 8,294 psi) while maintaining low GWP (192 kg CO₂/m³). Demonstrates the power of HRWR to unlock low W/B without sacrificing workability in high-SCM systems.
79: Pure cement (667/0/0) at high W/B = 0.50 cured at 22°C. Achieves only 6,138 psi at 28 days — the high water content creates excessive capillary porosity. With the highest GWP (514 kg CO₂/m³) and modest strength, this represents the baseline that SCM substitution aims to improve upon.
81: Fly-ash-dominant (400/267/0) at W/B = 0.50 without HRWR. The 40% fly ash replacement reduces GWP to 319 kg CO₂/m³ but only achieves 5,379 psi at 28 days. The high W/B and lack of slag limits strength development — compare with slag-containing mixes at similar SCM levels that reach much higher strengths.
